title: Your dog has a dosha
folder: W1-01 - Sun 18 Oct - Your dog has a dosha

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Watch them for one evening and you'll know.

The one who hates the cold, startles at the pressure cooker and gets gassy after a new treat. The one who eats like it's a race and loses patience at 6pm. The one who would happily nap through a wedding.

Ayurveda has read bodies this way for about 3,000 years. It calls the pattern a constitution, or dosha: Vata (air and space), Pitta (fire and water), Kapha (earth and water). Veterinary herbal medicine texts (R. Silver DVM, Veterinary Herbal Medicine, 2007) describe the same constitutional reading for dogs, and holistic vets use it to decide what to watch for in a particular animal.

It is not a diagnosis. It is a lens, and it tells you what tends to go wrong first for your dog, so you notice earlier and tell your vet sooner.

Try this tonight: watch where they sleep, how fast they eat and what sets them off. By bedtime the answer is usually obvious.

So, which one is at your feet right now? Comment V, P or K, and tag the friend whose dog is 100% Pitta.

title: The dry-fruit box
folder: W1-05 - Thu 22 Oct - The dry-fruit box

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Diwali is 17 days away and the dry-fruit box is already on the coffee table.

Six festive foods, ranked by how fast they can hurt a dog, with what to watch for (ASPCA Animal Poison Control, VCA Animal Hospitals, Merck Veterinary Manual).

Raisins and grapes (the kishmish in every box): vomiting, low energy, not eating. Even a few can cause kidney failure in some dogs. Toxic.
Chocolate (barfi, anyone?): vomiting, restlessness, racing heart, tremors. Dark and baking chocolate are the worst. Toxic.
Onion and garlic (namkeen, dal, sabzi leftovers): weakness and pale gums, often days later. Raw, cooked or powdered, they damage red blood cells. Avoid.
Xylitol (sugar-free sweets and gum): signs within an hour, from vomiting to collapse. Check labels, even on peanut butter. Emergency.
Macadamia nuts (the party bowl): weakness in the back legs, vomiting, tremors. Other nuts are too fatty anyway. Toxic.
Alcohol (drinks left on the floor): wobbling, vomiting, slow breathing. Even small sips are dangerous. Never.

If they ate something on this list, in this order: note what, how much and when, and keep the wrapper. Call your vet or an emergency clinic now; don't wait for signs. Don't make them vomit unless the vet says so. And save your vet's number in your phone today.

title: Pet parents have ten heads too
folder: DUS3 - Tue 20 Oct - Pet parents have ten heads too

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Pet parents have ten heads too.

Ravana was not stupid. He was the most learned man of his age. His problem was ten heads talking at once: when his own brother told him to give Sita back, nine heads shouted him down, and he never heard the one quiet voice that could have saved him.

Anyone who loves a dog knows the feeling. One quiet body in the house that cannot speak, and ten loud heads of our own worrying over it at 2am.

Tonight the city burns Ravana. We burn nine of ours and keep the one that listens.

1. "Is that limp nothing, or something?" Watch three days, write it down, then call. Ayurveda calls it nidana: look before you act.
2. "He ate a kaju katli. Will he die?" Call the vet, not Google. One kaju katli is usually a tummy ache. Raisins, chocolate and xylitol are the emergencies.
3. "I was gone all day. Does he think I left?" He forgave you at the door. Dogs live in the greeting, not the absence.
4. "He's slowing down. Is this the end?" Slower is usually sore, and sore can be helped. It is a conversation with your vet, not an ending.
5. "Am I doing enough?" You are reading this with a dog asleep against your knee. Ravana never asked that question once.

The one we keep: noticing. Where they sleep, how fast they eat, what changed this week. Every good decision starts from that head.

A footnote for Dussehra: the most loyal creature in the whole epic was not a man.

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Show us your dog's Diwali look. The Best-Dressed Dog contest is open, and it's judged by the dog.

A bandana counts. A kurta counts. A single marigold on the collar counts. What wins is a dog who looks comfortable in it, because that is the only look that was ever worth a photo.

Three rules before the outfit goes on, straight from the people who see the fallout (RSPCA Australia; American Kennel Club):

1. He could take it off himself. Loose enough to walk, sit, sleep and pee in. Nothing over the eyes, ears, nose or mouth. No safety pins, no dangling bits.
2. Five minutes, then off. Photos, treats, done. Body costumes trap heat, and a Diwali evening is warm before the excitement starts.
3. Read the face. Soft eyes, ears up, easy mouth: happy. Freezing, pawing at it, ears flat, panting: off it comes. You already have the photo.

How to enter: DM the photo to @ayurpetofficial, or post it and tag us with #BestDressedDogAyurPet. Add their name and one line about the look, and follow @ayurpetofficial. Entries close Sunday 1 November, 11:59 pm IST. We shortlist on 2 November, you vote from 3 to 6 November, and the winner is announced on 7 November.

title: Festive dressing: Comfort is the look
brief: Comfortable, pet-safe festive dressing guidance (fit, heat, no loose ties or beads, short wear time, watch for stress signs).

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Before the kurta goes on the dog, read his ears.

Festive dressing can be sweet or a quiet ordeal, and the difference is small. Six rules, from the RSPCA's welfare guidance and the American Kennel Club:

1. Why vets wince at full costumes: a body costume traps heat, can stop normal walking and resting, and hides the signals that he needs to go out.
2. The five-minute rule: photos, treats, off. Never leave him unattended in it; costumes shift, snag and become chew toys.
3. Nothing on the face. A safe outfit never interferes with seeing, hearing, breathing, walking or resting. Hats and masks fail the test.
4. No dangly bits. Buttons, gems and loose decorations get swallowed and can lodge in the airway or gut. Glitter and dyes irritate skin. Safety pins never touch a dog.
5. Read the face. Panting indoors, freezing, pawing or biting at the outfit, ears flat, whale eye: off, immediately.
6. The Ayurveda layer: some dogs run hot by nature. Pitta dogs, the big-appetite, short-fuse ones, overheat first. Heavy fabric plus a warm evening plus excitement adds up. For them, cotton, or just a marigold on the collar.

Comfort is the look. If you want the photo, introduce the outfit a few days early, keep it to minutes, and reward with treats.

title: Sleeping position weather report

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Look at them right now. The way they're lying down is a weather report.

Belly up, legs everywhere: they're releasing heat. Paw pads and the belly carry little fur, so exposing them cools the body fast, and it also says "I feel safe here" (American Kennel Club, Dr Jerry Klein). The tight donut keeps heat in and guards the belly; you'll see more of it on cold nights. Flat out with legs behind is the ready position puppies and high-drive dogs love. Curled against you is warmth plus trust.

title: He steals your warm spot
folder: W1-03 - Tue 20 Oct - He steals your warm spot

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Every single morning. You stand up, and he slides into your warm spot before your feet hit the floor.

Most of us were told that's dominance, a dog trying to be the boss of the bed. The American Kennel Club calls that an urban legend. The truth is softer and a lot more interesting.

The spot you left is the warmest, most you-smelling place in the house. Staying close to your heat and your scent is the whole point.

Does sharing the bed cost you sleep? Less than you'd think. A Mayo Clinic study tracked 40 adults for a week: sleep efficiency was 83% with the dog in the room, and about 80% with the dog on the bed (Patel et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2017). Small study, no control group, but the message is clear: most people sleep fine.

Our extra layer: heat-seeking is a tell. Dogs that hunt warmth all winter lean Vata in Ayurvedic terms, and warm bedding, warm food and a fixed routine suit them.

Give them their own bed if they growl or stiffen when you reclaim the spot (that's a vet and trainer conversation, never punishment), if they're small or senior and leaping off a tall bed, or if your allergies flare at night. Otherwise: up by invitation, and the spot stays yours.

Turmeric is the most searched herb for dogs, and most of it is wasted.

Here's what the research actually says, in five lines.

1. Curcumin is real. Turmeric's curcuminoids are anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; that much is well established in people and in the lab (Int J Mol Sci, 2023 review).
2. Almost none gets absorbed. Curcumin barely dissolves in water and is broken down fast. On its own, very little reaches the blood.
3. A pinch of haldi in food mostly passes through. Kitchen turmeric is only a few percent curcumin, and it's dry and unpaired.
4. What helps: fat, pepper, extract. Curcumin is fat-soluble, and piperine from black pepper raised absorption about three-fold in studies.
5. The dog trial: promising, not magic. In a placebo-controlled trial (Innes et al., Veterinary Record, 2003), vets rated dogs on a turmeric extract as improved, while the force-plate measure didn't change.

Ask your vet first if your dog is on blood thinners, has surgery coming up, or has gallbladder or liver problems. High doses can upset the stomach. Dose by body weight, never by the spoon.

This is why Hip-O-Joint+ is a liquid: a 95% curcuminoid extract paired with boswellia, in drops you dose by weight. It supports joint comfort and mobility; it is not a treatment, and your vet should know about everything your dog takes.

title: Caring for an old dog
folder: W1-06 - Fri 23 Oct - Caring for an old dog

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
If you've been quietly exhausted lately, this one is for you.

Caring for an old dog is tiring, and science finally named it: caregiver burden. A Kent State University study (Spitznagel et al., Veterinary Record, 2017) surveyed 238 owners and found that people caring for a pet with a chronic or terminal illness reported more stress, anxiety and depression, and a lower quality of life, than owners of healthy pets. You are not weak, and you are not imagining it.

Why it adds up: night checks, pills, slow laps around the block. Each one is small. Together they are a second job that nobody sees, including you.

The trap: "just old age" hides pain. Slower on stairs, fussier with food, flinching when touched. Senior care guidelines (AAHA) are clear that many age-related changes are pain, and pain can be treated. Tell your vet exactly what the daily routine costs; they can only treat what you report.

The lens we add: old age is a Vata season in Ayurveda. Dryness, stiffness and restlessness rise with age. Warmth, routine and gentle movement are the daily medicine.

Try this tonight: write the routine on one page. Circle the task that drains you most. Ask one person to take it for a week.

Comfortable joints are part of the answer, and that is what Hip-O-Joint+ (boswellia and turmeric extract, in drops) is for. It supports joint comfort and mobility; it isn't a treatment, and your vet stays in charge.

title: That face is not guilt
folder: W1-07 - Sat 24 Oct - That face is not guilt

captions.ayurpetofficial_india:
Before anyone in the family says "bad dog", look at the face again.

That face isn't guilt. It's fear. Dogs say "I'm uncomfortable" quietly, long before they growl. Here are the five whispers (American Kennel Club; Cornell Riney Canine Health Center).

Whale eye: the whites of the eyes showing. Calmly give space and remove what's bothering them.
The lip lick: a quick lick with no food around is often a stress signal, not hunger.
The stress yawn: a yawn in a tense moment (vet, guests, crackers) means "I'm uneasy", not "I'm sleepy".
Ears back, tail tucked: that's fear. Move them away from the trigger. Never scold a frightened dog.
The stress ladder: lip lick, yawn, look away. Then whale eye, ears back, tail tucked. Then stiff body, growl. Then snap or bite. Every rung was a request to stop.

Never punish a growl. It is a request for space, and punishing it teaches a dog to skip the warning next time.
